prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Madness, Guy, Debord

outputs.L1:
Madness “hath builded her house in the high places of the city.” — Guy Debord

Men hang themselves soundlessly in the dark hours before the bottle shop opens, rope snaking over a pepper-tree branch at the lodging house. An empty tenement. Dark windows bruised by sky, illuminating rookeries of collapse and fire, crumbling outward until the whole street lies vacant and mud-caked.

In the ragged brown of summer verticordia, I urinated near a midden of fleshy arils heaped at an anthill entrance and watched them drag seed deep, instilling acacia into the dirt.

The withering of certainty spits, hisses. The swamps fill with drill holes guarded by adders. The air churns with a fierce screaming: warra! Warra. A dumbbell of yield and sequence.

Through years of discipline, I learned containment—or vice versa—as natural as speech. An upward spiral of spell. A nested equivalence, this woundedness. Pinned fury petering into honeyeater as a falcon plucks its way to the warm core, feathers wafting down to soft eremophila.

Sentences in the Bible begin with And God, as if beginning were difficult and well populated: an excess of tangle and downcast in need of a name.

The roof rats went quietly once the python escaped to the ceiling rafters of my father’s house, its coagulation of coils echoing the shapes of a nearby bogong moth.
outputs.L2:
“Madness has raised her dwelling on the city’s heights.” — Guy Debord

Before the liquor store unlocks, in the blackest part of morning, men end their lives by hanging, without making a sound.  
At the boarding house, a rope winds over a pepper-tree limb.  
The tenement stands deserted, its windows dark, stained by the sky.  
Bird-haunts of ruin and flame break apart and fall away, until the entire street lies empty, crusted with mud.  

In summer’s torn brown verticordia, I urinated beside a refuse heap of soft arils piled at the mouth of an anthill.  
I watched the ants haul the seeds down into the earth, planting acacia in the soil.  

Certainty dries out, then spits and hisses.  
The wetlands are being crowded with drill holes, each watched over by adders.  
The air twists with a savage cry: warra! Warra.  
A paired weight of harvest and order.  

Across years of training, I learned restraint—or perhaps restraint learned me—until it seemed as ordinary as speech.  
A charm climbs in a spiral.  
This injury folds into itself as a layered sameness.  

Rage, fastened in place, fades inside a honeyeater while a falcon tears inward toward the bird’s warm center, and feathers drift down onto the soft eremophila below.  

In the Bible, sentences open with “And God,” as though beginning were hard, and already crowded with presences.  
Too much knotting, too much lowered gaze, all waiting to be named.  

The roof rats disappeared without fuss after the python slipped into the ceiling beams of my father’s house, its thickened loops repeating the forms of a bogong moth nearby.
outputs.L3:
The text presents a bleak and unsettling urban landscape, one marked by suicide, abandonment, physical decay, and social collapse. Its world appears damaged at every level: buildings deteriorate, human lives are interrupted or discarded, and the city itself seems to carry the traces of violence and neglect. Rather than offering the city as a place of order, community, or progress, the text depicts it as a space of exhaustion and breakdown. The presence of suicide and abandonment gives the landscape an emotional weight, suggesting not only material ruin but also a deeper psychic and social despair.

At the same time, the imagery of insects, plants, birds, snakes, and swamps complicates this vision of collapse. Nature is not absent from the ruined urban environment; instead, it persists within it, pushing through or lingering alongside the signs of human damage. These natural images suggest survival, adaptation, and recurrence, even in places shaped by violence. However, nature is not presented as purely comforting or restorative. The insects, snakes, and swamp imagery also carry associations of danger, decay, and unease. In this way, the natural world becomes both a sign of endurance and a reminder that life continues in forms that may be unsettling, indifferent, or predatory.

The speaker’s reflections on woundedness, containment, discipline, and uncertainty deepen the text’s sense of instability. To be wounded is not simply to suffer; it is to become aware of the body’s vulnerability and of the difficulty of maintaining boundaries. Containment suggests an attempt to hold pain, memory, or disorder within limits, while discipline implies the force required to impose structure on experience. Yet uncertainty remains central, preventing any stable resolution. These states are not separate but deeply intertwined: injury produces the need for containment, containment requires discipline, and discipline is undermined by doubt. The speaker’s consciousness therefore mirrors the damaged landscape, moving between control and disintegration.

Biblical and philosophical references further frame the act of making meaning as difficult and unstable. Ideas of creation and naming evoke the possibility of bringing order into chaos, as in biblical acts of origin where the world is formed and named. Yet in this text, such acts do not appear simple or authoritative. Naming does not fully secure meaning, and creation is shadowed by destruction. Philosophical reflection likewise emphasizes the uncertainty of interpretation: to name something is not necessarily to understand it, and to impose meaning may reveal the fragility of meaning itself. The text therefore questions whether language can truly organize a world marked by suffering and decay.

The final image of the python and the moth gathers many of these concerns into a single disturbing scene. The python suggests predation, constriction, and primal force, while the moth evokes fragility, attraction, and transformation. If the image is connected to domestic memory, it brings danger into the intimate space of recollection, making the home or the past feel unstable rather than secure. The moth may suggest metamorphosis or vulnerability, while the python embodies the threat of being consumed or contained. Together, they create an atmosphere of unease in which memory, nature, and violence become inseparable. The ending does not resolve the text’s tensions; instead, it leaves the reader with an image of life caught between transformation and destruction, intimacy and threat.
outputs.L4:
The text unfolds as a fragmented meditation on despair, decay, violence, and ecological entanglement. Its language is imagistic rather than linear, moving through broken scenes in which bodies, landscapes, animals, plants, and sacred references appear in close and unsettling proximity. Human suffering is not presented as separate from the natural world, but as something embedded within it: ruin enters the soil, blood mingles with growth, and the damaged body becomes part of a wider field of organic and symbolic transformation.

Throughout the work, images of human collapse are juxtaposed with animal presences, vegetal life, and biblical motifs. These elements create a dense atmosphere in which violence feels both historical and elemental. The wounded landscape becomes more than a backdrop for human pain; it becomes an active participant in that pain, absorbing it, reflecting it, and continuing beyond it. Animals suggest instinct, endurance, and vulnerability, while plants evoke both burial and regeneration. Biblical echoes deepen the sense of judgment, exile, sacrifice, and naming, giving the poem a mythic dimension even as it remains rooted in physical decay.

The text does not offer consolation in any simple sense. Instead, it suggests that suffering and survival are bound together in a cycle that cannot be easily separated. Collapse is not an ending alone; it is also a process through which matter changes form, names are given or lost, and life persists in altered states. Violence leaves marks, but those marks become part of the terrain. The landscape is scarred, yet it continues to grow. The body is wounded, yet it remains connected to other bodies, species, histories, and forms of life.

In this way, the text presents devastation as inseparable from continuity. Its fragmented structure mirrors the brokenness it describes, while its recurring natural and sacred images imply that even ruin participates in a larger pattern of transformation. The world it imagines is harsh, unstable, and haunted, but not empty. Within decay there is still movement; within despair there is still naming; within destruction there is still the strange persistence of life. The wounded landscape becomes a site where death and growth, violence and renewal, human grief and ecological survival remain deeply intertwined.
outputs.L5:
**Madness and Guy Debord**

Madness, in the work and legacy of Guy Debord, is not simply a psychological condition. It is also a social and political atmosphere: the madness of a world that has replaced lived experience with images, commodities, and spectacle. Debord, the French theorist, filmmaker, and founding figure of the Situationist International, became famous for his 1967 book *The Society of the Spectacle*, in which he argued that modern capitalist society no longer organizes itself only around production and consumption, but around representation. Life is increasingly mediated by images. People do not merely live; they watch life being displayed to them.

For Debord, this condition produces a kind of collective delirium. The spectacle turns reality upside down: appearances become more important than truth, passivity replaces action, and human relationships are filtered through commodities and media. In such a society, madness may appear as individual breakdown, but Debord suggests that the deeper insanity belongs to the system itself. A world that asks people to find meaning in advertising, celebrity, status, and endless consumption is already irrational.

Debord’s critique also carries a tone of refusal. He was not interested in adapting peacefully to the spectacle. Instead, he wanted to expose it, disrupt it, and recover authentic experience. The Situationists experimented with practices such as the *dérive*, or drifting through urban spaces, as a way to escape the routines imposed by capitalist city life. They sought moments of freedom, play, and intensity against a society that reduced people to spectators.

Madness, then, can be read in two ways in relation to Debord. On one hand, there is the madness of the spectacle: a normalized insanity hidden beneath everyday life. On the other hand, there is the “mad” refusal to accept that world as inevitable. To reject the spectacle may look irrational to those who have accepted it completely. But for Debord, true reason begins with recognizing the absurdity of the world we are told is normal.

In this sense, Guy Debord remains important because his ideas feel even more relevant in the age of social media, constant advertising, digital identities, and permanent visibility. The spectacle has not disappeared; it has become more intimate and more continuous. Our lives are increasingly measured through images, profiles, screens, and performances. Debord’s work asks whether this is progress—or whether it is a sophisticated form of madness that we have learned to call reality.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, surreal prose poem in a bleak Australian landscape, blending Guy Debord-style social decay, biblical cadence, ecological imagery, and memories of lodging houses, suicide, birds, snakes, and insects.
counterfactuals.output:
At the edge of the saltpan, where the bitumen loosens into heat and the heat into hallucination, the lodging house rises in memory like a condemned ark: fibro walls, rusted flywire, a corridor smelling of boiled mutton, disinfectant, damp socks, and the slow arithmetic of failed men. There were rooms there with numbers nailed crookedly to the doors, and in each room a small republic of ruin—one chair, one bed, one basin stained brown beneath the tap, one mirror in which the face returned as evidence. We watched television in the common room as if awaiting revelation, but the screen gave only weather, sales, wars elsewhere, girls selling beer with the radiance of angels trained in commerce. And behold, the whole world had become a shopfront after closing, lit from within by dead fluorescent tubes, and no one knew how to enter except by debt.

Outside, the country lay opened like scripture scorched at the margins. Mallee roots gripped the red earth with the patience of prophets. Crows arranged themselves on the telephone wires, black notes in a hymn to vacancy, and galahs rose at dusk in a pink confusion, as though embarrassment itself had taken wing. The river had retreated into its own name. Fish bones glittered in the cracked mud. Ants carried the empire grain by grain beneath our boots. Locust shells clung to fenceposts, transparent masks of hunger, and flies baptised every wound with their small, persistent benediction.

In those days we spoke of suicide softly, as one speaks of rain in a drought: not as desire, always, but as weather approaching across the plain. A man from Room 7 stopped appearing at breakfast. A woman with a rosary tattooed on her wrist stared all afternoon at the railway line until the freight train passed through her without touching her. Another fellow kept a brown snake in a pillowcase and called it Mercy, feeding it mice he trapped behind the bins. At night we heard it slide inside the wall of his room like a thought that had found a body. The cockroaches came out after lights-out, polished and priestly, moving among our crumbs as if administering an old covenant: from dust thou art rented, and unto dust thou shalt be evicted.

The landlord collected envelopes on Fridays. His keys chimed like coins in a beggar’s dream. He had the eyes of a tired butcher and the soul of a turnstile. In the kitchen, beneath a calendar of a beach no one could afford to visit, we made tea the colour of creekwater and watched moths burn themselves against the bulb, each one a tiny industry of longing. The nation beyond the verandah kept multiplying its mirrors—billboards, screens, betting shops, shopping centres cooled to the temperature of morgues—until even loneliness became a product with a logo and the poor were invited to purchase their own disappearance in weekly instalments.

And yet the land did not believe in us. It endured our slogans, our subdivisions, our plastic saints. The termites wrote their blind gospels inside the beams. The ibis probed the dump with the solemnity of monks. Magpies rehearsed their silver arguments before dawn. A goanna crossed the road like an ancient question no parliament could answer. Above the paddocks, storm clouds gathered but withheld judgement, bruised and biblical, while lightning stitched white scars into the belly of the sky.

O desolate commonwealth of asbestos and spinifex, of Centrelink queues and empty dams, of men asleep in boots and women folding grief into sheets; O caravan parks of exile, O boarding houses of the last supper, O towns where the pub is the temple and the bottle shop its vestry; we have eaten the dust of spectacle and called it bread, drunk the neon and called it wine. We have mistaken display for daylight, possession for mercy, noise for the voice in the wilderness.

Still, in the morning, the insects begin again. The birds divide the air. The snake leaves its script across the sand and vanishes under corrugated iron. Somewhere a door opens in a lodging house and someone, not yet dead, steps out into the hard Australian light, carrying nothing but a cup, a cigarette, a memory of feathers, and the terrible unfinished mercy of being seen by no one.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental long-form poem with no clear stanza breaks, using fragmented syntax and apocalyptic imagery: bottle shops, abandoned tenements, acacia seeds, drillholes in swamps, honeyeaters, falcons, pythons, and a father’s house.
counterfactuals.output:
At the lip of the bottle shop the evening unthreads itself,  
fluorescent, insect-buzzed, a saint with a cracked halo,  
and the men go in and out carrying amber weather,  
small storms in paper bags,  
their mouths full of rusted hymns,  
their hands remembering other hands,  
doors that closed,  
keys lost in the ash of suburbs.  
No clear road now.  
No map but the receipt curling in the gutter.  
No moon but the security camera, blind and swivelling,  
counting the last coins of the world.  

Abandoned tenements lean inward like exhausted witnesses,  
windows punched out, stairwells smelling of rainwater, urine, old cooking oil,  
rooms where mattresses bloom with mildew,  
where a child’s shoe hardens beside a dead refrigerator,  
where wallpaper peels in long tongues,  
speaking of rent, eviction, fever, the small catastrophes  
that arrive before the final one.  
In the walls: wires gnawed into nerves.  
In the ceiling: nests of dust.  
In the courtyard: a shopping trolley full of black rain.  
Someone has written FATHER in blue paint across a door  
and underneath it HOUSE  
and underneath that nothing,  
only brick, only the continent’s red silence pressing through.  

Acacia seeds sleep in a jar on the windowsill,  
hard little planets, little sealed commands,  
waiting for fire to speak their names.  
Waiting for the world to burn correctly.  
A grandmother once said they outlast us,  
the seeds, the stones, the stories buried sideways in the tongue,  
but the tongue dries, splits, forgets its own water.  
The jar falls.  
Glass among the cockroaches.  
Seeds scatter under the couch, under the bones of the floor,  
into the cracks where ants go carrying crumbs of apocalypse,  
sweetly, efficiently, without prophecy.  

And somewhere beyond the last bus route  
drillholes fill with swampwater,  
dark mouths cut into the green lung of the earth,  
iron teeth of the rig withdrawn but not forgiven.  
The swamp exhales methane, scripture, mosquitoes.  
Reeds bend over the punctures as if listening  
for the old gods trapped below the clay,  
for coal, for gas, for the slow black money of buried forests.  
Men in hard hats vanish in the heat shimmer.  
Survey flags flutter like warnings from a country already dead.  
Each hole a question.  
Each question leaking.  
Each leak a hymn no one will admit to hearing.  

Honeyeaters arrive at dawn,  
stitched from yellow nerve and restless sugar,  
beaks probing the bruised blossoms,  
their throats clicking with tiny alarms.  
They know the air has changed.  
They know before the ministers, before the screens, before the fathers  
standing in kitchens with their backs to the children,  
staring into sinks as if the plumbing might explain history.  
The honeyeaters dart through smoke haze,  
bright scraps of refusal,  
feeding in the acacia as embers fall around them  
soft as unmailed letters.  

Above, falcons carve the heat.  
One circle, then another,  
a blade rehearsing the shape of hunger.  
They look down on the bottle shops,  
the tenements, the roads buckling, the pools gone green,  
the father’s house with its iron roof ticking under firelight,  
its veranda sagging like an old jaw,  
its rooms arranged around a silence too large to furnish.  
Falcons do not forgive.  
Falcons do not remember the names of sons.  
They read only movement,  
the tremor in grass,  
the rabbit-heart,  
the city-heart,  
the last nation twitching beneath tin.  

In the swamp a python slides through drillwater,  
muscle written in oil,  
scale by scale the old alphabet returning.  
It coils around a drowned fencepost.  
It tastes diesel on the air.  
It carries in its body the patience of before houses,  
before fathers, before doors made sacred by fear.  
Its tongue opens the dark like a key.  
Somewhere a generator fails.  
Somewhere a siren becomes a bird and flies into smoke.  
Somewhere the radio says evacuation evacuation evacuation  
until the word becomes a dry seed,  
until the seed becomes a tooth,  
until the tooth bites down on the soft fruit of the century.  

Father’s house at the end of the gravel road.  
Not home.  
Never home.  
A structure of weathered boards, tax letters, rifles locked in a cabinet,  
cups ringed with brown tea,  
a shed full of nails in jars,  
fuel cans, rope, a calendar of horses from a year no one survived intact.  
The hallway smells of dust and menthol.  
The bedroom curtains are shut against noon.  
On the table: a loaf gone blue, a bill, a knife,  
three acacia seeds in the palm of an ashtray.  
In the yard: bones of machinery,  
grasshoppers snapping from the grass like sparks.  
In the roof: possums.  
In the walls: the soft industry of termites  
composing their patient sermon.  

I come back because the roads behind me are burning.  
I come back because the city has lifted its black wings.  
I come back carrying no offering but my mouth,  
broken cup, cracked bell,  
mouth full of bottle-shop neon, tenement dust, swamp rot,  
mouth full of honeyeater panic, falcon shadow, python sleep.  
Father sits on the veranda and does not ask.  
His hands are maps of failed rain.  
His eyes two drillholes where the swamp has risen.  
Between us the afternoon hangs, gutted,  
flies walking over its shining insides.  
He says the fires will turn.  
He says they always do.  
He says this land needs burning.  
He says nothing about the children.  

Behind the house the acacias begin to ignite,  
first one pod splitting, then another,  
small shots in the heat,  
seeds flung into the future with no consent from us.  
The honeyeaters scatter, shrill and golden.  
The falcon climbs through a bruise of smoke.  
The python, unseen, enters the cool dark under the floorboards  
where father’s boots wait,  
where the old newspapers curl,  
where all the lost keys of the house lie green with corrosion.  
The bottle shop explodes in town,  
brief cathedral of glass and alcohol,  
and the tenements answer with their hollow organs,  
room after room lighting up,  
windows singing without voices.  
The swamp takes the drillholes back into itself  
or pretends to.  
Black bubbles rise.  
The earth opens one eye.  

No clear stanza.  
No clean ending.  
Only the house breathing heat through its seams.  
Only father asleep in the chair or dead or pretending.  
Only my hand on the doorframe,  
feeling the grain lift under ash,  
feeling the old timber remember forest,  
feeling the forest remember fire,  
feeling the fire remember seed,  
feeling the seed remember rain  
that may not come,  
that may come too hard,  
that may come as nails, as frogs, as black water through the vents,  
as government notice, as birdbone, as silence.  

Night.  
If it is night.  
The sky has the colour of a wound held open.  
Stars falling like slag.  
Honeyeaters dreaming in the smoke with their tiny engines cooling.  
Falcons folded into the burnt air.  
Pythons knotting the foundations.  
Acacia seeds everywhere, under tongue, under nail, in the pockets of the dead,  
in the gutters outside the bottle shop,  
in the stairwells of abandoned tenements,  
in the drillholes, in the swamp’s black throat,  
in father’s house,  
in father’s ashtray,  
in father’s closed fist,  
hard, bright, waiting,  
as if the end of the world were only another kind of germination.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dark modernist prose-poem that opens with a quotation from Guy Debord and moves through scenes of urban collapse, outback flora and fauna, religious language, and personal childhood memory.
counterfactuals.output:
“Separation is the alpha and omega of the spectacle.” — Guy Debord

At dusk the city loosens its bolts. Towers lean into their own reflections, glass grieving glass, while the avenues fill with a black rain of receipts, ash, and pigeon feathers. The billboards keep shining after the power fails, lit by some interior doctrine of hunger. In the subway, the turnstiles revolve for no one, accepting the small coins of the dead.

Beyond the last service station, the bitumen gives up. The outback begins like a wound refusing to close: spinifex bristling in the heat, saltbush silvered with dust, mulga trees bent in the posture of old prophets. A red kangaroo stands at the roadside, immense and still, as if appointed to judge the wreckage. Galahs shriek above the rusted water tank. A goanna slides through the noon like a thought too ancient to confess.

Lord of vacant lots, have mercy. Lord of cracked reservoirs, receive our signal. We built our churches from shopping centres and called the escalators ascent. We knelt before refrigerated light, before the immaculate fruit, before the sermon of discount and display. Now the roof has opened. The rain falls through the nave. The mannequins wear soot for vestments.

I remember being a child in the back seat of my father’s car, the vinyl hot against my legs, the world passing in fragments: petrol smell, cicada scream, my mother’s hand reaching back with a peeled orange, its little moons wet and bright. I believed then that distance was a form of promise, that every road led toward a house with a lamp on. Now the roads return bearing only dust, animal tracks, and the thin blue smoke of extinguished suburbs.

Night gathers in the broken city and the desert at once. The elevators sleep between floors. The eucalypts shed their bark like saints discarding skin. Somewhere a magpie rehearses its liquid, metallic psalm. Somewhere a child, not yet instructed in ruin, presses a face to the window and mistakes the burning skyline for dawn.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a gritty, imagistic poem in the style of contemporary Australian eco-poetics—violent, elliptical, philosophical, with references to madness, suicide, mining, native plants, birds of prey, ants, adders, and biblical beginnings.
counterfactuals.output:
**GENESIS WITH TAILINGS**

In the beginning: not light,  
but a drill-bit worrying the dark  
like a bad tooth.

The earth opened its red mouth.  
Men climbed in with lamps  
and came out silvered, coughing,

their names eaten first  
by payroll, then by dust.

Spinifex stitched the horizon shut.  
Saltbush held its grey hands up—  
not surrender, not prayer,

only the old arithmetic  
of thirst.

A wedge-tailed eagle circled  
the mine’s torn scripture,  
reading the thermals

for carrion, for consequence.  
Below, the ants kept carrying  
their black commas

through the sentence of the day.

Who was the first madman?  
Adam, naming everything  
as it fled him?

Eve, hearing the serpent  
hiss from the rootwork  
of a dead mallee?

Or God, splitting void from void  
and calling the wound good?

At noon the heat became a verdict.  
Kangaroo bones shone  
beside the haul road.

The creek, once a throat,  
now clicked with stones.  
Adders braided themselves

through the copper grass,  
each one a small theology  
of venom and patience.

Somewhere a man walked out  
past the last ute, past the dog fence,  
past the range’s purple bruise,

carrying in his head  
a room with no door.  
The sky did not stop him.

It merely burned.

At dusk the pit filled with shadow.  
Not water. Never water.  
Only the counterfeit mercy

of darkness pouring down  
the benches, the blasted steps,  
the ore-body’s exposed nerve.

Still the grevillea flared—  
red tongues in the ash.  
Still the banksia held its cones

like grenades of future fire.  
Still the ants entered the carcass  
and made of it a city.

O country, butchered mother,  
iron-veined and fly-blown,  
you do not forgive.

You germinate.

And under the dragline’s rusted jaw,  
under the eagle’s black wheel,  
under the first lie ever spoken—

that we were given dominion—  
the seeds wait, hard as teeth,  
dreaming rain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an avant-garde poetic passage about societal ruin and inner containment, mixing Situationist epigraph, rural Australian natural detail, family memory, and strange observations of animals, using a fragmented, incantatory voice.
counterfactuals.output:
*“Beneath the pavement, not the beach—  
but a buried instruction for escape.”*  
—after the Situationists

The town collapses inward first,  
not with sirens,  
not with parliament ash,  
but with the soft administrative rot  
of men signing forms in rooms without weather.

A magpie clicks its black-and-white machinery  
on the fencepost.  
The paddock, yellowed to bone,  
holds the heat like a secret punishment.  
All afternoon the eucalypts shed their skins—  
long grey ribbons, priestly, useless—  
and the creek, reduced to a chain of brown mirrors,  
keeps reflecting nothing back.

We were taught containment early.

Grandmother’s hands in the laundry tub.  
Blueing in the rinse.  
A cake tin full of buttons, each one  
a small moon fallen from a dead shirt.  
My father at the kitchen table,  
silent as a sealed well,  
peeling an orange in one unbroken spiral  
while the news spoke of markets, borders, fire.

Outside, sheep moved like thoughts  
that had forgotten their thinkers.

I say society and hear corrugated iron.  
I say ruin and hear the windmill turning  
though no water rises.  
I say inner life and a fox  
steps delicately through the chook yard at dawn,  
red as an accusation,  
carrying an egg unbroken in its mouth.

O spectacle of the empty main street.  
O fluorescent butcher, O bank with its blind glass.  
O children learning to desire the cage  
because the cage is lit from within.

The ants have found the sugar.  
The crows have found the lamb’s eyes.  
A goanna lies flattened on the bitumen,  
ancient script of its body interrupted  
by the grammar of tyres.

Mother kept photographs in a shoebox:  
weddings, floods, a cousin in uniform,  
a baby held up to the sun  
as though being offered to weather.  
In every picture someone is squinting.  
In every picture the horizon waits  
with its mouth shut.

We built rooms inside our chests.  
We locked the rooms.  
We called the locks character.  
We called the walls love.  
We called the small high window  
a future.

At dusk the galahs descend—  
pink, ridiculous, holy—  
screaming in the dead gum  
like a committee of angels gone wrong.

And still the earth insists:  
spinifex, burr, saltbush, dust;  
the rabbit’s nervous scripture  
stitched under the fence;  
the dam’s cracked lip;  
the moon rising over the silo  
like a white tablet no one can swallow.

Do not ask who ruined the world.

We did it by staying calm.  
We did it by paying bills.  
We did it by inheriting silence  
and polishing it for guests.

Inside me: a cupboard.  
Inside the cupboard: a child.  
Inside the child: a matchbox.  
Inside the matchbox: one green beetle,  
alive, astonished,  
tapping its lacquered head  
against the dark.
